preamble: The shift from the voiced bilabial stop [b] to the vowel [u] (realized as the offglide of a diphthong) is a form of vocalization. In the history of Western Romance, Latin /b/ in syllable-final position (before a consonant, often after loss of an intervening vowel) weakened through a fricative stage [β] and then lost its consonantal closure, yielding diphthongs such as [au], [eu] and [ew]. The change is well documented but largely confined to Ibero-Romance and Occitano-Romance.

examples.note: Via older Spanish absente; coda /b/ before /s/ vocalized, giving the diphthong au.
After syncope, coda /b/ before /d/ vocalized to [u].
After loss of the post-tonic vowel, /b/ before /r/ vocalized, yielding the diphthong [ɛw].
Syncope of the post-tonic vowel put /b/ before /l/, where it vocalized to [u].
Same syncope-plus-vocalization development as in Catalan.
